intro_questions.title: Knowledge Questions
intro_questions.description: These questions test your knowledge of MLOps and ML related concepts and principles. We will ask you to answer the same questions again when you have completed the serious game session to measure your learning progress.
intro_questions.question: What is 'concept drift' in the context of Machine Learning?

answers.text: **Model accuracy declines over time** as real-world data gradually shifts or trends change.
The model's **code becomes incompatible** with updated software libraries over time.
**Intentionally shifting parameters** during training to prevent vanishing gradients.
A **security attack** that plants subtle biases in training data to trigger specific failures.

intro_questions.question: What is the difference between Machine Learning (ML) and Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) ?

answers.text: ML covers **model creation and evaluation**; MLOps covers **deployment, monitoring, and production maintenance**.
ML is **theoretical algorithm design**; MLOps is only **empirical testing and tuning**.
ML handles **data exploration and training**; MLOps is a **one-time handoff** to operations.
ML **maximizes accuracy** on isolated datasets; MLOps focuses on **feature engineering and data augmentation**.

intro_questions.question: What does the MLOps principle of 'Reproducibility' ensure?

answers.text: An experiment gives **identical results** when repeated with the same data and environment.
**Tracing a prediction back** to the exact data and code version that produced it.
**Automatically re-running training** whenever input data shifts significantly.
**Consistent performance metrics** across multiple validation datasets.

intro_questions.question: What impacts could unmanaged pipeline complexity (pipeline jungles) have?

answers.text: **Hard to trace which data version** trained a deployed model, making results difficult to reproduce or debug.
**Hyperparameter search grows harder** with each added pipeline, degrading performance.
**Deployment slows down** as each new step needs approval before serving.
**Monitoring gets harder** as alerts spread across many pipelines, delaying fixes.

intro_questions.title: Stakeholder Perspective
intro_questions.description: These questions describe how someone in a project might act or think, without naming their job. Pick which role fits best.
intro_questions.question: When last Tuesday's numbers don't line up with the week before, they want to know exactly why the input changed, not just whether the forecast at the end still looks reasonable.
When someone proposes a new project, they want to know which number on the weekly report would actually move, and by how much, before agreeing to spend a cent on it.
After doing the same release steps by hand for the second time, they start quietly scripting it away, even though nothing has broken yet and nobody asked them to.
Even after everyone agrees the results look good, they still want to see it walked through every rule that was written down months ago before anyone calls it done.
Even when the input hasn't changed at all, they'll keep adjusting the model's settings until its mistakes stop looking so avoidable.
They're the one who finds out, mid-afternoon, that the thing which was fine this morning has quietly stopped working for actual users right now.

intro_questions.title: Trade-off Scenarios
intro_questions.description: These describe a disagreement between two roles on a project similar to yours. Pick the best answer for each.
intro_questions.question: A regional distributor needs a restocking feature shipped before a two-day cold-chain audit deadline. The production engineer wants to ship now with a manual sign-off instead of the full automated acceptance-test suite. The compliance architect insists every release passes the automated suite first, even if it slips the deadline. Which resolution best matches how such trade-offs are usually handled?

answers.text: They agree on an **interim check** now, with the **fuller process** following shortly after.
They wait for the **full process** to finish, even past the agreed date.
They go ahead **without raising it** with the other side at all.
They **leave the call** to someone who wasn't part of the original disagreement.

intro_questions.question: A cold snap threatens frozen-goods demand forecasts. The business analyst needs a stock decision within the hour. The data engineer wants to pause integrating a new weather feed into the pipeline until it's validated, worried a rushed integration corrupts the pipeline. What is the underlying tension here?

answers.text: **Needing to act** before all the facts are confirmed, against **wanting to confirm** them first.
Doing more **by hand** against doing more **automatically**.
Whether the newer feed can be **trusted** at all, regardless of timing.

intro_questions.question: Marketing wants a personalized-discount model live before a big promotion week, built on customer loyalty-card data. The DevOps engineer could deploy today by skipping the staged rollout. The compliance architect wants the standard review done first, since loyalty data is personal data under consent rules. Which role is most likely to treat this as non-negotiable regardless of the deadline, and why?

answers.text: The one responsible for **data-handling rules**, not something traded for speed.
The one who could **ship it today**, since once something's built, finishing it becomes the priority.
The one pushing for the **promotion deadline**, since marketing timing rarely moves.
None of them; there's a **workable middle ground** here too.
